content.intro: This lesson covers What Is the Rust Programming Language?. It sits in Module 1, Introduction to Rust, and builds toward a practical Rust mental model rather than memorizing a term in isolation.
content.why_it_matters: What Is the Rust Programming Language? matters when you work with language goals and project trade-offs. Understanding the rule helps you predict compiler or runtime behavior, document assumptions, and choose a safer implementation when inputs or system conditions change.

Start with the smallest example, identify the inputs and assumptions, and check the edge cases before using the technique in a larger program.

content_blocks.title: A reliable way to reason about it
content_blocks.text: For What Is the Rust Programming Language?, write down the inputs, the guarantee you expect, and the boundary where that guarantee stops. Work through a minimal example first; then deliberately test one edge case. Rust is a compiled language designed around explicit control and compile-time safety checks. Trade-offs depend on a project’s performance, interoperability, hiring, and delivery constraints.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake and recovery
content_blocks.text: Do not assume What Is the Rust Programming Language? guarantees more than it actually does. Reduce a failure to a small reproducer, read the full compiler diagnostic or error value, consult the matching official reference, and change one assumption at a time.

content_blocks.title: Toolchain and execution boundary
content_blocks.text: Course examples are static reference snippets, not executed inside CodeLeaf. Most standard-library examples can be tried in a Rust 2024 Cargo project; specialized networking, database, async, procedural-macro, embedded, and WebAssembly scenarios require the toolchain and dependencies described in their lessons.
